edges.effect_quant: In a cardiac ICU cohort of 144 adults treated off-label with atypical antipsychotics for delirium or agitation, adverse events occurred in 25% of quetiapine recipients versus 6% of olanzapine recipients, with QTc prolongation in 18% versus 6%. A 12-case review of quetiapine-associated QTc prolongation found torsades de pointes in 4 cases, almost always in the presence of additional risk factors.
edges.population: older or medically complex adults receiving off-label quetiapine for delirium, agitation, insomnia, or other non-psychotic indications in acute-care settings
edges.mechanism: Quetiapine can inhibit cardiac repolarization through hERG-related effects, especially when combined with electrolyte abnormalities, CYP3A4 interactions, structural heart disease, or other QT-prolonging drugs. Off-label use often occurs in medically fragile settings where those cofactors cluster.
edges.summary: Off-label low-dose quetiapine is not a high-frequency torsades drug in the way ziprasidone is, but it does carry a real QT-prolongation signal that becomes clinically relevant in frail or cardiac patients. The most defensible interpretation is that the average absolute risk is modest, yet clearly non-zero and amplified by comorbidity and co-prescribing.
edges.caveats: Much of the evidence comes from observational or case-based data rather than dose-finding randomized trials in older adults. Apparent harm often depends on baseline QT risk, concurrent QT-prolonging drugs, overdose, or metabolic interactions, so this edge should not be read as a uniform large effect in all low-dose users.
